name: Two Pointers and Sliding Window
intent: Turn pair and substring problems from quadratic to linear by moving two indexes instead of restarting, and know the condition that makes it valid: each move must safely rule something out, which fails as soon as negative numbers or a non-monotone condition arrive.
scenario: A report must find two prices in a sorted list that add up to a budget, and the longest run of days whose total spend stays under a limit. The first draft tries every pair and every start: fine on the 100-row test file, 49,995,000 checks on the 10,000-row production file. A rewrite with a sliding window is instant, until a month of refunds (negative amounts) arrives and the fast version quietly returns a shorter run than the truth.
problem: Nested loops over pairs or ranges cost n squared, and they redo work: when the loop moves on to the next start it forgets everything it learned about the last one. Two pointers and the sliding window keep that knowledge in the position of two indexes and a running total, so each element is touched a constant number of times. But the technique is a proof in disguise. It is only correct when moving a pointer can never skip the answer, and that depends on the data: sortedness, or numbers that are all positive.

howItWorks.title: Two pointers from the ends of a sorted list
howItWorks.text: To find two numbers that add up to a target in a sorted list, put one pointer at the smallest item and one at the largest. If their sum is too small, the smallest item cannot pair with anything left (the largest remaining partner is already too small), so move the left pointer up. If the sum is too big, the largest item cannot pair with anything, so move the right pointer down. Every check rules out one item for good, so the search costs at most n - 1 checks: 999 for 1,000 items where trying every pair costs 499,500. The sorted order is what makes each move safe.

howItWorks.title: A window that grows and shrinks
howItWorks.text: For a run of neighbouring items, keep a window from l to r and a running total. Move r right to add an item, and while the total breaks the rule, move l right to drop items. Each item enters the window once and leaves at most once, so the work is at most 2n steps whatever the window size: 19,900 for 10,000 positive numbers and a limit of 500, where trying every start costs 1,001,650. The same shape finds the longest substring without a repeated character (the window keeps a count per character) and the shortest stretch that covers a set of needed items.

howItWorks.title: Why it is correct: every move rules something out
howItWorks.text: Skipping work is only legal if the skipped candidates cannot be the answer. With positive numbers, once the window from l to r is over the limit, every longer window starting at l is over it as well, so l can be abandoned for good. Say that sentence in a comment: it is the whole proof. The gain is also bounded by the problem: the brute force stops early when stretches are short, so a limit of 50 makes trying every start cost 106,615 steps rather than a million. The window wins by roughly half the window length (it does 2 steps per item, the brute force about one per item in the window), not always by a factor of n.

howItWorks.title: Break it: negative numbers
howItWorks.text: Allow numbers below zero and a total can come back down when more items are added, so a window that is over the limit may still contain a longer stretch that works once a later item arrives. The shrink step throws that start away. The code still runs, still takes about 2n steps, and returns an answer: on 1,000 numbers between -3 and 5 and a limit of 500 it says 502 where the true longest run is 506. Nothing crashes, so only a test against the slow version catches it. Correct approaches for such data exist (typically prefix sums plus a sorted or monotone structure, around n log n), but they are a different algorithm, not a patch.

howItWorks.title: What you need before reaching for it
howItWorks.text: Check three things. The data is ordered or monotone in the way the move needs: sorted for the two-end version, non-negative for a sum window, a condition that only gets worse as the window grows. The question is about contiguous items or pairs, not arbitrary subsets. And the cost of preparing the data is counted: an unsorted list costs n log n to sort first, and a hash set finds a pair in one pass with extra memory instead. When the conditions hold, the idea reduces a quadratic scan to linear, which at 1,000,000 items is the difference between about 8 minutes and a millisecond at one step per nanosecond.

pros: Linear time: each item is visited a constant number of times, with 2n steps at most for a window
Constant extra memory beyond a running total or a small count table
Short code: two indexes and a loop
Works as a streaming algorithm for windows: items can be consumed once as they arrive
cons: Correctness depends on a property of the data (sorted, non-negative, monotone) that is easy to lose later
A violated assumption gives a plausible wrong answer, not an error
Covers contiguous ranges and pairs, not arbitrary subsets or combinations
Sorted input is required for the pair version, so unsorted data pays n log n first
whenToUse: A pair or triple in a sorted list that meets a sum condition
The longest or shortest contiguous range under a limit, with non-negative numbers or a count of distinct items
Merging two sorted lists, partitioning in place, or removing duplicates from a sorted list
Rolling statistics over the last N items of a stream, with a fixed or variable window
whenNotToUse: Data with negative numbers when the rule is a sum limit, unless you have proved the moves are still safe
Unsorted data, when a hash set solves the pair problem in one pass and the extra memory is acceptable
Subsets that need not be contiguous, which usually need dynamic programming or search
Very small inputs, where nested loops are shorter and easier to review
pitfalls: Using a sliding window on data that can be negative: the shrink step assumes the total only grows, so on 1,000 numbers from -3 to 5 with a limit of 500 the window answers 502 instead of 506, quickly and without any error

Testing only with a target that sits early in the pair order: trying every pair found it in 1,997 checks for 1,000 items, so a slow version looks fine; also test with a target that does not exist, where it needs 499,500

Believing a sliding window is always faster by a factor of n: the brute force costs about n times the window length when sums only grow, so with short windows (a limit of 50) it needed 106,615 steps for 10,000 items against 19,990 for the window
Counting a loop inside a loop as quadratic without checking: a while loop that moves l inside a for loop that moves r looks nested but each pointer only moves forward, so the total is at most 2n

Moving the wrong pointer on a tie or at the boundary, or using < where <= is needed: the loop skips a pair or reads outside the list; write down what each move rules out and check both pointers at n = 1 and n = 2
Forgetting to subtract the item that leaves the window from the running state: a total or count that only ever grows makes the shrink loop run away or stop too early
Running two pointers on a list that is not sorted: the move that 'rules out an item' is false, and the pair is missed; sort first (n log n) or use a hash set
Assuming a window is contiguous in the original data when the data was reordered, filtered or paged: a window over a sorted copy is not a window over the log

roles.label: Caller
roles.description: Asks for a pair, or the longest run under a limit.

roles.label: The numbers
roles.description: A sorted list, or a sequence that may or may not have negative values.

roles.label: Left pointer
roles.description: The start of the window, or the smallest candidate.

roles.label: Right pointer
roles.description: The end of the window, or the largest candidate.

roles.label: Running total
roles.description: The sum or count kept for the window, updated one item at a time.

quiz.question: A sorted list has 1,000 items and no pair adds up to the target. Roughly how many checks do two pointers need compared with trying every pair?
options: About 500,000 checks against about 1,000, since pointers revisit items.
About 10 checks against about 1,000, since the list is halved each time.
About 1,000 checks for both, since each item must be seen once.
quiz.explanation: Each check moves one pointer past an item that can no longer be part of a pair, so at most n - 1 = 999 checks are needed. Trying every pair needs n(n-1)/2 = 499,500. Halving is binary search, a different technique that does not apply to this two-end walk.

quiz.question: A sliding window for the longest stretch with sum at most K is run on data that now includes negative numbers. What happens?
options: It becomes quadratic, because the left pointer has to restart.
It raises an error as soon as the total drops below zero.
It stays fast but can return a stretch shorter than the true longest one.
It returns the right answer, but needs about twice as many steps.
quiz.explanation: The shrink step assumes that dropping the left item from an over-limit window is safe, which holds only if the total never comes back down. With negatives it can, so a start that would have worked is abandoned. The loop still takes at most 2n steps and returns a number, which is why the bug is silent.

quiz.question: Why is a while loop that moves the left pointer inside the for loop that moves the right pointer still linear overall?
options: Because the inner loop always runs exactly once per outer step.
Because each pointer only moves forward, so the inner loop's total moves are at most n.
Because the compiler turns the inner loop into a constant-time lookup.
Because the inner loop works on a copy of the window, not the original.
quiz.explanation: The left pointer never goes back, so across the whole run it moves at most n times in total, however many of those moves happen during one outer step. That gives at most n + n steps. It is the same kind of argument as in amortized analysis: count the total, not the worst single iteration.
